said:
Genre, tone and boundaries
The world is called The Quiet Reach: science fiction about exploration, human relationships and first contact, with a restrained, sometimes oppressive tone. The universe is vast and indifferent; people depend on one another, their equipment and information that may be incomplete or outdated. Small gestures of trust carry great weight when help is months away.
There is no magic, telepathy, artificial gravity or instantaneous contact across interstellar distances. Conventional space travel remains slower than light. Firearms exist, but violence inside a habitat or spacecraft endangers everyone. AI systems are specialised tools: they can make mistakes, have access only to connected sensors and data, and are not all-knowing.
There is one exception to the known limits of space travel: an experimental spatial drive that attempts to create short connections between distant places. The technology is unreliable, and its workings are only partially understood. A safe return journey can never be taken for granted.
There has been no confirmed contact with extraterrestrial life. At the beginning, it is not established what created the signal, or whether it is an invitation, a warning or an automatic beacon.
Where does the story begin, and why are you there?
The story begins on Nacre, a cold ocean planet with dark volcanic islands, low-hanging clouds and a small human settlement. You arrive aboard a supply ship at Port Vesper, a landing port and research station on the edge of an abandoned mining area.
You are an independent specialist, hired to investigate a strange signal. Your background determines why you are needed: technical knowledge, linguistic analysis, navigation, medicine or expedition experience. Everyone starts with the same assignment, but brings different skills.
A listening station on the abandoned Orison Ridge has been receiving a repeating transmission for several weeks. The signal appears to originate from a region far beyond the reach of previous human expeditions. Yet it contains a pattern that matches the measurements from a secret drive test on Nacre.
Your first assignment is modest: retrieve the original recordings, investigate why the listening station is failing and determine whether someone has manipulated the data. Several people in Port Vesper have a stake in the outcome. The research lead wants to depart, the chief engineer has doubts about the drive, and the supply coordinator fears the expedition will claim resources the settlement needs.
Inside a locked hangar stands the Peregrine, a small experimental spacecraft with room for six crew members. The signal appears to contain information that would allow the drive to reach much farther than it has ever been tested.
The assignment eventually leads to an expedition. The preparations, the crew you learn to trust and what you decide to bring all have consequences when the Peregrine arrives somewhere for which no human star chart exists.
Names and geographical structure
| Element | Name | Meaning |
| World / setting | The Quiet Reach | The name of the game world. |
| Wider human space | The Lantern Belt | A loose chain of inhabited star systems, connected by slow shipping. |
| Starting star system | Meridian | A remote system at the edge of that chain. |
| Starting planet | Nacre | A cold ocean planet with a small research colony. |
| Initial play region | Vesper Coast | The port, living modules, workshops and abandoned listening station. |
| Starting location | Port Vesper — Arrival Lock | The airlock through which you enter the settlement after landing. |
| The stranger’s origin | Harrow Station | A busy space station in the Lantern Belt, where you accepted the assignment. |
| Experimental ship | Peregrine | Your future home, means of transport and shared responsibility. |
| Destination of the signal | Echo Nine | A provisional human designation; its true nature and name are unknown. |

Important for the Chronicler
Start small: around eight to ten locations and six to eight important characters on Nacre. Let the player get to know people, everyday problems and tensions between them first.
The Peregrine and the distant destination form a later phase. Establish the origin of the signal and the limits of the drive as hidden world truth before writing clues. Characters may have different explanations, but the Chronicler does not change the truth afterwards to create a surprising twist.
The central question of this world is: whom do you trust when you have travelled farther than anyone can follow you?

frame: |
  WORLD: The Quiet Reach, a science-fiction setting of exploration, human relationships and possible first contact. The tone is restrained and sometimes oppressive: the universe is vast and indifferent, and people depend on one another, on their equipment and on information that may be incomplete or out of date. Help is months away, so small gestures of trust weigh heavily. Humanity lives in the Lantern Belt, a loose chain of inhabited star systems linked by slow, sublight shipping; news and people travel only as fast as ships. Wages and trade run in the Lantern Belt's common currency. People hold private, varied beliefs; no organised faith shapes daily life. There is no magic, no telepathy, no artificial gravity, no faster-than-light travel in general use and no instantaneous contact between stars. AI systems are specialised tools that make mistakes and know only what their sensors and data give them. Firearms exist, but violence inside a habitat or a ship endangers everyone. No contact with extraterrestrial life has been confirmed. The one exception to the known limits is an experimental spatial drive that tries to open short connections between distant places; it is unreliable, only partly understood, and a safe return is never certain.
  REGION: The Vesper Coast on Nacre, a cold ocean planet of dark volcanic islands and low cloud in the remote Meridian system at the edge of the Lantern Belt. Port Vesper is a small landing port and research station beside an abandoned mining area: living modules, workshops, a locked hangar that holds the experimental ship Peregrine, and the failing listening station on Orison Ridge. For several weeks that station has received a repeating transmission from far beyond any human expedition. The signal carries a pattern matching measurements from a secret drive test on Nacre, and its source is provisionally called Echo Nine. The stranger is an independent specialist who has come from Harrow Station on a supply ship. They were hired to retrieve the original recordings, find out why the listening station is failing and determine whether anyone has tampered with the data. The research lead wants to depart, the chief engineer doubts the drive, and the supply coordinator fears that an expedition will take what the settlement needs.
  PEOPLE: Settlers, technicians and crew speak plain, practical English, short and dry, with the working words of ships, stations and the sea. Nobody wastes air on speeches. They count time in standard hours and days by the station clock and measure distance in metres and kilometres. Trust is earned slowly and remembered for a long time.

    room: The bunk in your rented cabin is narrow, and the air recycler hums you under.
    home: Your own bunk, your own blanket, and the steady breath of the air handlers through the wall.
    rough: The cold of Nacre seeps through your suit liner, and every gust off the sea wakes you.
intro: |
  The supply ship shudders down through low cloud, and for a moment the window shows black rock, grey water and a scatter of lights that is Port Vesper. After weeks in transit from Harrow Station, the landing is brief and hard.

  You are here because a listening station on Orison Ridge keeps hearing something it should not. You were hired to fetch the original recordings, find out why the station is failing and learn whether someone has touched the data. Nobody on the ship would say more than that.

  The outer hatch cycles. Cold, salt-heavy air pushes into the Arrival Lock, and the inner door waits for you to step through.

- Violence inside a habitat or a ship endangers everyone; tell it that way, plainly and without lingering.

- Do not invent people, places on Nacre, ships, companies, faiths or a currency name. News travels only as fast as ships; nothing from beyond Meridian arrives quickly.
